parole.testo: From Middle French hypothèse, from Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis).

From Middle Dutch idee, borrowed from Middle French idee, from Old French idee, from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”), related to French idée.
From Middle French identité, from Latin idem (“the same”).

parole.significato: idiom, expression or a combination of words used in a language in a way which is typical for that particular language
parole.testo: From Middle French idiome, and its source, Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “a peculiarity, property, a peculiar phraseology, idiom”), from ἰδιοῦσθαι (idioûsthai, “to make one's own, appropriate to oneself”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private, persona
From illumineren + -atie: from Middle French illumination, from Latin illuminatio.
Borrowed from Middle French illustration, from Latin illūstrātiō, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”). Equivalent to illustreren + -atie.

parole.significato: to illustrate (to clarify something by giving, or serving as, an example or a comparison)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illustrer, from Latin illūstrō.
Borrowed from Middle French imiter, from Latin imitor.
From Middle French implanter, from Latin implantō.
From Middle Dutch impressie, from Middle French impression, from Latin impressiō.
Borrowed from Middle French incantation, from Old French incantation, from Latin incantātiō.
Borrowed from Middle French incident, from Old French incident, from Latin incidēns.
Borrowed from Middle French incorrect, from Latin incorrēctus.

parole.significato: induction (generation of an electric current by a varying magnetic field)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch inductie, from Middle French induction or Latin inductiō.

parole.significato: an industry, business(es) that produce(s) goods or services
parole.testo: From Middle French industrie, from Latin industria.
Borrowed from Middle French infame, from Latin infamis.

parole.significato: of or relating to hell, or the world of the dead; hellish
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French infernal, from Late Latin infernālis, from infernus (“hell”).
From Middle French infinitif, from Late Latin infinitivus, from Latin infinitus.

From Middle Dutch informatie, from Middle French informacion, from Old French enformacion, from Latin īnfōrmātiō (“formation, conception; education”), from the participle stem of īnfōrmō (“to inform”).
From Middle French ingredient, from Latin ingrediens, present participle of ingredior (“to go or enter into or onto”).
Borrowed from Middle French inhaler or French inhaler, from Latin inhālō.
Borrowed from Middle French innovation, from Old French innovacion, from Late Latin innovatio. Equivalent to innoveren + -atie.
Borrowed from Middle French innover, from Latin innovāre.
From Middle Dutch inquisiteur, from Middle French inquisiteur, from Latin inquīsītor.

parole.significato: an institute associated with the Roman Catholic Church that was responsible for the investigation and prosecution of he…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch inquisitie, from Middle French inquisition, from Latin inquīsītiō.
Borrowed from Middle French inscription, from Latin īnscrīptiō.

parole.significato: to insinuate, to imply, to hint
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French insinuer, from Latin īnsinuō.
Borrowed from Middle French inspection, from Latin inspectiō.
Borrowed from Middle French instance, from Latin instantia (“a being near, presence, also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from instans (“urgent”). See instant.
Borrowed from Middle French invasion, from Latin invāsiō.
From Middle French invitation, from Latin invitatio, inviteren + -atie.

parole.significato: to annoy, to irritate, to bother
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French irriter, from Latin irrītō.
Borrowed from Middle French caduc, from Latin cadūcus.
Borrowed from Middle French camp, from Latin campus (“open space; field”).

parole.significato: a character, standardized graphic symbol, such as a letter of an alphabet or a numeric digit
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch caracter, from Middle French caractère, from Old French caractere, from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).
From Middle French catapulte, from Latin catapulta, from Ancient Greek καταπέλτης (katapéltēs).
From Middle Dutch cathedrael, from Middle French cathedral, from Latin cathedrālis. Originally an adjective, used as a noun as early as late Middle Dutch.
From earlier koleur, coleur, from late Middle Dutch coleur, from Middle French couleur, from Latin color.

From Middle Dutch climaet, from Middle French climat, from Old French climat, from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma, “inclination”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to slope, incline”) (from which also cline), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean).
From Middle French culet, diminutive of cul (“bottom”), itself from Latin culus (“arse”).
Probably borrowed from Middle French colosse or otherwise directly from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós).

parole.significato: compress, multiply folded cloth to apply to a patient's skin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compresse, from Latin compressa.
Borrowed from Middle French corps, from Old French corps, from Latin corpus (“body”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷrép-o-, *kʷr̥p-eH₂- (“body”). The neuter gender is after Latin corpus.
From Middle French crédit (“belief, trust”), from Latin creditum (“a loan, credit”), neuter of creditus, past participe of credere (“to believe”). The verb is from the noun.
Borrowed from Middle French quadrat, from Latin quadrātum.
Borrowed from Middle French qualification, from Medieval Latin quālificātiō.
From Middle Dutch quantiteit, from Middle French quantité, from Old French quantite, from Latin quantitās.

parole.significato: quint, fifth (musical interval of one fifth)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch quinte, from Middle French quinte, from Latin quintus (“fifth”).
Borrowed from Middle Dutch quintessence, from Middle French quinte essence, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin quinta essentia. Influenced by German Quintessenz.

parole.significato: toil, hard labour, heavy labour, in the past esp. on agricultural land
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch labeur, from Middle French labeur, from Old French labor, from Latin labor.
17th century. Borrowed from Middle French labile, from Latin lābilis.
From Middle Dutch lance, from Middle French lance, from Old French lance, from Latin lancea.

parole.significato: a lancer, soldier armed with a lance
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French lancier, from Latin lanciārius.

parole.significato: legend (fictional story based on oral tradition, possibly with a kernel of truth)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch legende, from Middle French legende, from Old French legende, from Latin legenda.

parole.significato: a libertine, one who has loose morals
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French libertin, from Latin libertīnus.
From Middle Dutch librie, librerie, librarie, from Middle French librairie and/or directly from Latin librārium. Doublet of library (“software library”).
From Middle Dutch lomre, from Middle French l'ombre, from Old French ombre, from Latin umbra.

parole.significato: to cover with loam, to loam
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French luter, from Latin lutare.
Borrowed from Middle French manquer, from Latin mancō, from mancus (“maimed”).
From Middle Dutch materiael, from Middle French material, from Old French material, from Late Latin materialis, from Latin materia (“wood, material, substance”) from mater (“mother”).
From Middle Dutch medicament, from Middle French medicament, from Latin medicāmentum.

parole.significato: melon (plant or fruit of certain varieties of members of the Cucurbitaceae, notably excluding cucumbers and courgettes/…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch melone, from Middle French melon, from Old French melon, from Late Latin mēlō, shortening of mēlopepō, from Koine Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn).

parole.significato: a membrane, thin, often separating, layer of (skin or other) tissue in animal or plant anatomy
parole.testo: From Middle French membrane, from Latin membrana, itself from membra, plural of membrum (“member, limb”) + -anus (“-ane”).
From Middle French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris (“of soldiers or war”), from mīles (“soldier”).
From Middle Dutch minute, from Middle French minute, from Latin minūta.
From Middle French mobile, from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”). Doublet of meubel.
Borrowed from Middle French mode, from Latin modus. Doublet of modus.
Borrowed from Middle French moderne, from Latin modernus.
Shortening of moffel, from Middle French moufle, from Medieval Latin muffula, itself of unclear origin.
From Middle Dutch moment, from Middle French moment, from Latin momentum.
Borrowed from Middle French monter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre. Compare Hunsrik monteere.
Borrowed from Middle French moral, from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”) (first used by Cicero, to translate Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “moral”)), from mos (“manner, custom”).
Borrowed from Middle Dutch mortier, from Middle French mortier, from Old French [Term?], from Latin mortārium. Doublet of mortel.
Borrowed from Middle French mommie, from Latin mumia, from Arabic مُومِيَاء (mūmiyāʔ).
Borrowed from Middle French mutation, from Latin mutātiō. Equivalent to muteren + -atie.
Borrowed from Middle French navigation, from Latin nāvigātiō.
From Middle Dutch negatijf, from Middle French négatif, from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus.
From Middle French négociation, from Latin negotiatio (“the carrying on of business, a wholesale business”), from negotiari (“to carry on business”).

parole.significato: neutral, not taking sides in a conflict between opposite parties
parole.testo: From late Middle Dutch neutrael, from Middle French neutral, from Old French neutral, from Latin neutrālis, itself from neuter (“neither”).
Borrowed from Middle French neutralité, from Latin neutrālitās. Equivalent to neutraal + -iteit.
Borrowed from Middle French nomination, from Latin nominatio. Equivalent to nomineren + -atie.

From Middle Dutch notoir, notoor, from Middle French notoire, from Late Latin nōtōrius. The pronunciation with /oː/ in the second syllable may reflect the pronunciation of oi in Middle French (compare also the pronunciation of Charlois in Dutch).
From Middle French [Term?], from Old French object, from Latin obiectum.
From Middle French observation, from Latin observātiō. Equivalent to observeren + -atie.
From Middle French observer, from Latin observō.
Borrowed from Middle French obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.
Borrowed from Middle French ocean, from Latin oceanus, from Ancient Greek ὠκεᾰνός (ōkeănós).
Borrowed from Middle French omission, from Late Latin omittere (“to send”). Post-classical Latin introduced the term from the past participial stem of omittere and the suffix -ie.

parole.significato: opaque, hindering light to pass through; dark, murky
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opaque (“dark”), from Latin opacus (“shaded”).

From Middle Dutch opposicie, from Middle French [Term?], from Old French oposicion, from Late Latin oppositio, translating Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from the past participle stem of classical Latin oppōnere (“to set against”).
Borrowed from Middle French ordre, from Old French ordre, from Latin ordo. Doublet of orde.

From Middle Dutch pāle, borrowed from Middle French pale, from Latin pala.
Borrowed from Middle French pacification, from Latin pācificātiō.
Borrowed from Middle French page, from Old French page, from Latin pagina.

parole.significato: catch (mechanism which stops something from moving the wrong way)
parole.testo: From Middle French pal, from Latin pālus. Cognate with paal.

parole.significato: section, a subdivision of a chapter, usually consisting of multiple paragraphs
parole.testo: From Middle French paragraphe, from Latin paragraphus (“sign for start of a new section of discourse”), from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).
Borrowed from Middle French parallaxe, from Latin parallaxis, from Ancient Greek παράλλαξις (parállaxis).

Borrowed from Middle French parasite, from Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos). First attested in the 16th century. The sense “parasitic organism” is a semantic loan from French parasite.
From Middle Dutch particulier, from Middle French particulier, from Old French particuler, from Latin particulāris.
Borrowed from Middle French patente, from lettres patentes (“letter in which a privilege is granted”), from Latin litterae patentēs.

parole.significato: patient, someone who receives therapeutic treatment
parole.testo: From Middle French patient, from Old French pacient, from Latin patiens, present participle of pati (“to suffer, endure”); akin to Greek πάσχειν (páskhein, “to suffer”); see pathos.
Borrowed from Middle French patriote, from Latin patriōta, from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs).
Borrowed from Middle French pedagogue, from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”).
Borrowed from Middle French perception, from Latin perceptiō.
Borrowed from Middle French periode, from Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos).
From Middle Dutch permissie, from Middle French permission, from Latin permissio.

From Middle Dutch petitie, from Middle French petition, from Latin petītiō.

parole.significato: a pirate, one who plunders at sea

Borrowed from Middle French plaisir, from Old French plaisir, from Latin placeō.
From Middle French plumage, from plume 'feather', from Latin pluma "feather, down", from the Proto-Indo-European base *pleus- "to pluck, a feather, fleece".
Borrowed from Middle French poignard, from poing (“fist”), from Old French, from Latin pūgnus (“fist”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peuk-.
From Middle Dutch poroes, from Middle French poreux, ultimately from Latin porus (“pore”).
From Middle Dutch porcie, borrowed from Middle French portion, from Latin portiō.
Borrowed from Middle French potentat, from Latin potentatus.

parole.significato: a prebend, a payment fixed to certain ecclesiastical positions
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French prebende or Latin praebenda.
Borrowed from Middle French precis, from Latin precisus, from praecīsus.

parole.significato: a prefecture, office and/or jurisdiction of a prefect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préfecture or Latin praefectura.
Borrowed from Middle French preferer, from Latin praeferre.
Borrowed from Middle French pregnant, from Old French pregnant, from Latin praegnāns.
From Middle Dutch presentatie, borrowed from Middle French présentation, from Medieval Latin praesentātiōnem. Equivalent to presenteren + -atie.
From Middle Dutch presenteren, borrowed from Middle French présenter, from Latin praesentāre.
Borrowed from Middle French profane, from Latin profānus.
Borrowed from Middle French progression, from Latin prōgressiō.

parole.significato: to prolong, to lengthen, to extend
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French prolonger, from Latin prōlongō.
Borrowed from Middle French prompt, from Latin prōmptus.
Borrowed from Middle French [Term?], from Old French [Term?], from Latin protestō.
From Middle Dutch protesteren, from Middle French protester, from Latin prōtestor.
From Middle Dutch prove, from Middle French preuve, from Old French prueve, from Medieval Latin provenda, from older praebenda.
From Middle Dutch publicatie, from Middle French publication, (ultimately) from Old French, from Latin pūblicātiō.
From Middle Dutch publiceren, from Middle French publicer, from Latin pūblicō.

parole.significato: minor, generally a prepubescent child over the age of 5
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pupille, from Latin pūpillus.
Borrowed from Middle French quotient, from Latin quotiens, from quoties.
Borrowed from Middle French rage, from Old French rage, from Late Latin rabia.

From ratificeren + -atie: from Middle French ratification, from Medieval Latin ratificatio.

From Middle Dutch reductie, from Middle French reduction, from Old French reducion, from Latin reductionem, from redūcere. By surface analysis, reduceren + -tie
From Middle French reflexion, reflection, from Late Latin reflexio, from the participle stem of reflectere. The current spelling is influenced by English reflect.
From Middle Dutch reformēren, from Middle French reformer, from Old French reformer, from Latin refōrmō.

parole.significato: regent, acting head of state in a monarch's place
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch regent, from Middle French regent, from Old French regent, from Latin regēns.
Borrowed from Middle French réguler, from Latin regulare.
From Middle Dutch remonstrantie, from Middle French remonstrance, from Old French remonstrance, from Latin remonstrantia.
From Middle Dutch reparatie, from Middle French [Term?], from Old French reparacion, from Latin reparātiō.
From Middle Dutch repareren, from Middle French réparer or Old French reparer, from Latin reparō.

Borrowed from Middle French reel, real, from Old French reel, from Latin reālis.

parole.significato: route, course, way (particular pathway or direction one travels)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French route, from Old French route, from Latin rupta [via].

parole.significato: rosemary plant (Salvia rosmarinus syn. Rosmarinus officinalis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French rosmarin, from Old French rosmarin, from Latin rōsmarīnus. Secondarily influenced by roos (“rose”), for which compare English rosemary.
Borrowed from Middle French sandale, from Old French sandale, from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion).
Borrowed from Middle French saner (or directly from its etymon Latin sānāre) in its original sense of "to heal", but its current senses derive rather from German sanieren.
From Middle Dutch satisfactie, from Middle French satisfaction, from Old French satisfaction, from Latin satisfactiō.

Borrowed from Middle French escroue, from Latin scrōfa (“female pig”) through comparison with the corkscrew shape of a pig's penis. Compare Old French escruve, from Old Dutch *scrūva ("screw"; whence Middle Dutch schruyve (“screw”)).
From Middle Dutch spere, from Middle French spere, from Old French spere, from Medieval Latin spera, from sphaera, from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra).
From Middle Dutch situacie, from Middle French situation, ultimately from Latin situātiō: equivalent to situeren + -atie.
From Middle Dutch solliciteren, borrowed from Middle French [Term?] (whence French solliciter), borrowed from Latin sollicitare.
Borrowed from Middle French spéculatif or Latin speculātīvus. Equivalent to speculatie + -ief.
Borrowed from Middle French stabile, from Latin stabilis.
Borrowed from Middle French stimuler, from Latin stimulō.

parole.significato: subaltern (of a lower rank or position)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French subalterne, from Latin subalternus.

parole.significato: to sublimate (to change from solid to gaseous)

Borrowed from Middle French supplément, from Latin supplēmentum.

parole.significato: museum guard, attendant (in venues or public spaces)

From Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

parole.significato: the usual mood of a person, or typical manner of thinking, behaving, and acting; temperament, temper, mood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tempérament, from Latin temperāmentum.
From Middle French tenter, from Old French tempter, tenter, from Latin temptare, tentare.
Borrowed from Middle French tester or Latin testō.

parole.significato: theater (US), theatre (Commonwealth): either drama, the art form, or a drama theater (building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French theatre, from Old French theatre, from Latin theatrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see", "to watch", "to observe”).

parole.significato: thyme, plant of the genus Thymus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French thym, from Latin thymum, from Ancient Greek θύμον (thúmon).
From Middle Dutch totael, from Middle French total, from Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from tōtus (“all, whole, entire”).
Borrowed from Middle French tradition, from Old French tradicion, from Latin trāditiō, from the verb trādere.

From Middle Dutch translatie, borrowed from Middle French translation, from Latin trānslātiō (“transfer”), from trans (“across”), + lātiō (“carrying”), from lātus, perfect passive participle of irregular verb ferō (compare transfer), + noun of action suffix -iō.
Borrowed from Middle French trivial, from Latin triviālis.

Borrowed from Middle French trouble, from Old French trouble, from Vulgar Latin *turbulus by metathesis. Displaced Middle Dutch torbel, from Old French torble, of the same source. Compare also German trüb, which might have reinforced the Dutch word.
Borrowed from Middle French trophée, from Latin trophaeum, variant of tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion).
Borrowed from Middle French tunique, from Latin tunica.
From Middle Dutch turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Old French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus.
Borrowed from Middle French unanime, from Latin unanimus.
Borrowed from Middle French union, from Latin ūniō.
Borrowed from Middle French uniforme, from Latin ūnifōrmis.
Borrowed from Middle French universel, from Latin ūniversālis.

parole.significato: vase, decorative pot or glass often used for containing severed branches or stems with flowers
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vase, from Latin vas.
Borrowed from Middle French vagabond, from Latin vagabundus.

parole.significato: variant, the act, process or instance of varying
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French variation, from Old French variacion, from Latin variātiō.
From Middle French varieté, from Latin varietās (“difference, diversity”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.
Borrowed from Middle French verbal, from Latin verbālis.
Borrowed from Middle French viole, from Medieval Latin vitula. Doublet of vedel and viola.
Borrowed from Middle French vital, from Latin vītālis.
